tasks.title: clock sync test fails on SMP x86 whe running with QEMU
tasks.body:
Similar to QEMU ARM/RISC-V, `ENABLE_SMP_CLOCK_SYNC_TEST_ON_BOOT` should not be on for x86 QEMU. But since it's x86 the kernel doesn't know it's running on QEMU when you build the kernel for a generic x86 CPU.

According to my colleague @dreamliner787-9 there's no reliable way of looking at CPUID to tell if you're being virtualised by QEMU.

I'm wondering if anyone has any other ideas for how we could skip the test at run-time if we detect we're running on QEMU, I'm still getting familiar with the x86 architecture myself.

tasks.title: seL4_TCB_SetSchedParams: inconsistency between API reference and implementation
tasks.body:
For the seL4_TCB_SetSchedParams (MCS) invocation, the API reference states the following about the `sched_context` parameter

>  If the scheduling context is already bound to a notification or TCB that is not this TCB this operation will fail. Similarly, if this TCB is already bound to a scheduling context that is not this scheduling context, this will also fail.

This does not correspond to the implementation, which adheres to the following:

> If the scheduling context is already bound to a notification or TCB, this operation will fail. Similarly, if this TCB is already bound to a scheduling context, this will also fail.

In other words, the operation will fail if the scheduling context passed in is the one that is already bound to the TCB.

tasks.title: GCC 11.3 RISC-V ISA spec change from 2.2/20190608 to 20191213 might affect seL4
tasks.body:
In case we consider switching to GCC 11.3 or higher one day, we might run into this change causing problems:
- https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-11/changes.html
- https://gcc.gnu.org/git/?p=gcc.git;a=commit;h=98416dbb0a62579d4a7a4a76bab51b5b52fec2cd

There is a mail on the RISC-V SW-Dev mailinglist (sw-dev@groups.riscv.org) that describes the details (see also https://groups.google.com/a/groups.riscv.org/g/sw-dev/c/aE1ZeHHCYf4/m/v88QeovDAAAJ):

It’s Kito Cheng from the RISC-V GCC community, just sharing some news about the default ISA spec version that has been bumped to 20191213 on both RISC-V GCC and binutils recently, and that has one major incompatibility issue between current default ISA spec versions. The major incompatibility issue is the csr read/write (csrr*/csrw*) instructions and fence.i instruction has separated from the `I` extension, become two standalone extensions: Zicsr and Zifencei; so you might get error messages like that: unrecognized opcode `csrr`.
# How to resolve those issues?
Here is two solution to resolve:
- First one is what we recommend, adding zicsr and/or zifencei to your -march option, e.g. -march=rv64imac become -march=rv64imac_zicsr_zifencei
- The second one is a kind of workaround, using -misa-spec=2.2 to force RISC-V GCC using the older ISA spec version, however this is strongly  *NOT* recommended.
In case you want everything like before, you can add --with-isa-spec=2.2 build option for GCC and binutils, then the toolchain will default using the old version and work as an older GNU toolchain release.
# Why GCC/binutils bump that?
The default ISA spec version was set to 2.2 for long time, however the spec is released at May, 2017, which is 5 years ago, and RISC-V has at least two ISA spec release after that, so we believe that’s time to bump, and we also raise the discussion on the RISC-V BoF at Linux plumber, we reach a consensus is that we should moving forward even that having incompatible issue.
# Why bump that so late?
We worried about the incompatibility issue, but we realized that is unavoidable, and RISC-V is growing very quickly in the past year, so we believe it would be better to move forward now.
# Why is there an incompatibility issue there? Why can't you avoid that?
That is because the RISC-V ISA spec has changed, we believe the toolchain should honor what spec written.
# Which ISA spec versions are supported by GNU toolchain now?
Currently we support 2.2 20190608 and 20191213.
2.2: https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/releases/tag/riscv-user-2.2
20190608: https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/releases/tag/Ratified-IMFDQC-and-Priv-v1.11
20191213: https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/releases/tag/Ratified-IMAFDQC
# Is there any newer ISA spec supported? It’s 2022!
20191213 is already 2 years ago, but RISC-V didn’t have further formal ISA spec release after that, what we can promise is that RISC-V GNU toolchain will support soon if ISA spec has newer release.

tasks.title: document why it is Ok for some virtual kernel memory regions to overflow
tasks.body:
In #1002 and #389 we both stumbled over the fact that sometimes the function `create_untypeds_for_region` is being supplied with a region that overflows, i.e. where `end < start`.

This can happen when a valid physical memory region is translated to kernel virtual addresses. The overflow is harmless and is being handled gracefully by `create_untypeds_for_region` for device untypeds.

This is because the loop in that function splits the region into size-aligned chunks, and size-aligned chunks cannot themselves overflow, i.e. they will always satisfy `start <= end` (and because it checks for minimum size, actually `start < end`).

The overflow might also be harmless for normal untypeds as long as the resulting virtual addresses are in the kernel window.

All of this should be documented at least in the code, and since it is user visible possibly also somewhere in the manual.

tasks.title: Allow VMPIDR_EL2 register to be set for VMs when CONFIG_MAX_NUM_NODES=1
tasks.body:
Currently the seL4_VCPUReg enum only defines the seL4_VCPUReg_VMPIDR_EL2 register when the kernel is configured for SMP. This register should be available for unicore systems too as otherwise a user level VMM is not able to control the value of MPIDR_EL1 that the guest VM reads.

```
#if CONFIG_MAX_NUM_NODES > 1
    /* Virtualisation Multiprocessor ID Register */
    seL4_VCPUReg_VMPIDR_EL2,
#endif /* CONFIG_MAX_NUM_NODES > 1 */
```

tasks.title: MCS fault handling issue when specifying period of a TCB.
tasks.body:
This issue is related to VPPI faults on AArch64, which uses the fault handling mechanisms to deliver virtual PPI's to a single-threaded VM. Specifically, it was observed in an seL4 system built using Microkit where a virtual-machine-monitor services a Linux virtual machine. The `microkit` branch of seL4 was used with the Odroid-C4 and qemu-arm-virt platforms.

When specifying a period different to the budget of the TCB for the virtual machine and using the VPPI handling mechanism, we non-deterministically hit an assert in the ```tcbReleaseEnqueue``` function where our TCB is seemingly already in the release queue, and potentially shouldn't be at this point in time. The particular assert is here: https://github.com/seL4/seL4/blob/61a8ccef44eeb08ecd20ad40296340c8319adee5/src/object/tcb.c#L283

This issue doesn't occur when we set the period of the VM equal to our budget, and the thread is treated as a round robin thread.

My main suspicion is that the `postpone()` function, which in turn calls ```tcbReleaseEnqueue``` was getting invoked twice, but I have not been unable to completely validate this assumption. https://github.com/seL4/seL4/blob/61a8ccef44eeb08ecd20ad40296340c8319adee5/src/kernel/thread.c#L568 

Postpone is called from three places mainly https://github.com/seL4/seL4/blob/61a8ccef44eeb08ecd20ad40296340c8319adee5/src/kernel/thread.c#L614 
https://github.com/seL4/seL4/blob/61a8ccef44eeb08ecd20ad40296340c8319adee5/src/kernel/thread.c#L128
and
https://github.com/seL4/seL4/blob/61a8ccef44eeb08ecd20ad40296340c8319adee5/src/object/schedcontext.c#L284 

So the interrupting thread may be unable to refill or have insufficient refill available when trying to end its timeslice, handle a reply transfer or attempt to resume.

The naive and inconclusive fix for this was to switch the assert to an if statement, and return if the tcb was already in the release queue rather than hitting the assert. As the `tcbReleaseEnqueue` function places the thread into the release queue, which it already is in, I assumed this to be an ok behavior. However, this lead to other issues, such as hitting asserts stating the the thread is un-scheduable. 

This was the snippet added to `tcbReleaseEnqueue`:
```
    if (thread_state_get_tcbInReleaseQueue(tcb->tcbState) == true) {
        // Thread is already in queue,no need to queue again
        return;
    }
```
We have recreated this behavior in the simple example system at the following repository for both qemu-arm-virt and the odroidc4:

https://github.com/Kswin01/sel4cp_vmm/tree/mcs-bug

We have specified additional priority, budget and period for the VM thread inside of the system description files, as seen in the following commit: https://github.com/Kswin01/sel4cp_vmm/commit/14b3a5c388c1ecd222d313365bc46f5a6694b280.

tasks.title: x86: support to read out serial i/o ports from BIOS data area
tasks.body:
On Genode/x86 we use for all of our 7 supported x86 micokernels the BIOS data area to read out the serial configuration. This eliminates for us the need to manually finding out the I/O ports, which is especially handy on native machines you don't have next to you. Also the support of external users becomes comfortable since most the time the serial output 'just' works. We combine this mechanism with a small chained bootloader like bender [0, 1] that scans for PCI serial cards or/and Intel AMT SerialOverLine, writes it to the BIOS data area and then starts the actual microkernel.

What is your opinion about adding this BDA feature to seL4  in general ?

https://github.com/alex-ab/genode/commit/4c1fe8b2dbe4d7fed4c9f60bfa00822621e3f333 depicts the required changes, we currently apply manually to our Genode/seL4 version. (I decided for now to add extra cmdline options, which however are not strictly necessary for us.)

[0] https://github.com/genodelabs/genode/issues/768
[1] https://github.com/genodelabs/genode/issues/1625

tasks.title: Potential bug/vulnerability
Only one of `ARCH_{ARM,RISCV,ARCH_X86}` ever appears in `gen_config.json`
tasks.body:
Most kernel config options appear in `gen_config.json` whether or not they are enabled. They are associated with the value `true` if enabled and as `false` otherwise. `KernelSel4Arch`, for example, behaves this way.

`KernelArch` on the other hand, does not behave this way. For example, when configured for AArch64, `ARCH_ARM` is present in `gen_config.json` with the value `true`, but `ARCH_RISCV` and `ARCH_X86` are absent, instead of present with the value `false`.

Unlike C `#ifdefs` where the use of an undefined macro is allowed, the `#[sel4_cfg]` macro in Rust requires that the config keys exist. That means that the following will fail to compile on AArch64:

```rust
#[sel4_cfg(ARCH_RISCV)]
fn foo() {}
```

We are using the following verbose workaround:

```rust
#[sel4_cfg(any(ARCH_RISCV32, ARCH_RISCV64)]
fn foo() {}
```

The issue seems to be related to the use of choice conditions in the definition of the `KernelArch` option:

https://github.com/seL4/seL4/blob/f9eb65c9a586ccacb5d2583c1cf1882212bb592a/configs/seL4Config.cmake#L69-L76

tasks.title: riscv: place traps and fastpath code adjacently
tasks.body:
Follow Arm's code where it tries to place traps and vector
code adjacently in a 4KiB page to optimise performance
(through spatial cache locality).

This will also allow reducing the number of instructions
in the fastpath code by one by using conditional branches instead
of a check followed by a jump instruction. Though, if the future traps
or fastpath code got bigger than 4 KiB, this may fail linking again.

tasks.title: Cloned functions (-O2) are incompatible with binary verification
tasks.body:
`gcc -O2` enables various inter-procedural optimisations that can produce cloned or partial functions in the binary. These functions don't directly correspond to any function in the C, and are beyond the current abilities of binary verification.

For example, if GCC determines that part of a function is worth inlining, but the rest of the function is too big, it might split the function into parts, inlining the first, and emitting the second as a separate function with a new name ending in something like `.part.0`.

Adding `-fno-partial-inlining -fno-ipa-cp -fno-ipa-sra` seems to disable enough inter-procedural optimisations to avoid cloned and partial functions, at least with current kernel and compiler versions.

This issue is to discuss how and when these compiler options should be added to the kernel build. My initial suggestion would be to add the following to the bottom of `gcc.cmake`:

```
# Binary verification cannot handle cloned functions.
if(KernelVerificationBuild)
    add_compile_options(-fno-partial-inlining -fno-ipa-cp -fno-ipa-sra)
endif()
```

What do people think?

tasks.title: kernel/boot.c nitpick
Print memory regions as `[..)`
tasks.body:
At boot time we print memory regions as `[a..b]` even though `b` is not included in the interval.

This has confused me a number of times in the past, I suspect it is the same for others.

Correct [interval notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(mathematics)#Notations_for_intervals) would be `[a..b)`.

tasks.title: allow non-contiguous tag field in bitfield generator
tasks.body:
Context: on AArch64, the encoding for PTE types is context dependent: on level 3, a block PTE is signified by bottom bits `0b11`, but on levels 0-2, bottom bits `0b11` instead mean table PTE. 

For verification, we need a context-independent encoding of tagged unions. (And for general sanity).

Luckily there are 4 bits in PTEs that are reserved for software, so we can use one of these to indicate which kind of PTE we are talking about. The problem is that these bits live at positions `[58:55]`, and the type bits at `[1:0]`, so they don't form a contiguous field, which the current bitfield generator assumes.

With a relatively small extension, this could be made possible.  The extension would contain roughly the following steps/features:

- [x] extend parser to `tagged_union <type> <field>[:<field>]*`
- [x] each of these fields has to be in the same position and width in all blocks/alternatives
- [x] for simplicity, non-contiguous tags cannot be mixed with class-mask tags
- [x] tag mask = `or` of the masks of all tag fields
- [ ] enum = plain numbers (no shifting), e.g. `0b00010000011` where the first `1` is in a first field (e.g. one of those reserved bits) and the bottom `11` are in a separate field (e.g. the hardware type field)
- [ ] creation = as now, tag is a plain number, needs no masking or shifting
- [x] reading the tag = new combined function, works like normal field read, but with the overall tag mask
- [x] should not generate field functions (esp not `set`) for any tag field

Making the tag the `or` of all tag fields (masked) means there is no performance impact compared to the current bitfield code -- the same number of shifting/masking operations is happening after constant folding. It does mean that all tag fields have to be within the same word (e.g. can't be spread over `word[0]` and `word[1]` of a larger bitfield).

The bitfield proofs should be almost unchanged, but we will see more when we have a few examples.

Adding multiple words would be a performance impact (but only when they are used), and it would add a fair bit of complexity, including proof change, so this is best left for a separate stage if it is needed.

tasks.title: A specific  specific colorscheme is assumed
tasks.body:
# Problem

I just spent some time trying to debug my solution for the tutorial, when I found this: a spurious print of seL4 in green.

![image](https://github.com/seL4/microkit/assets/20400405/c90a832c-a004-4b24-8f7f-076acdfb6b2e)

Playing with the terminal, I finally found the following, crucial information:

![image](https://github.com/seL4/microkit/assets/20400405/b3ece8b4-329d-40a6-bf22-15d170a3cc15)

# Additional Information

For reference, my colorscheme is as following (generated using `terminal-colors -o`):

![image](https://github.com/seL4/microkit/assets/20400405/26e066d3-e345-4536-a494-bcaf00b83705)

# Cause

Now, investigating the [output](https://github.com/seL4/microkit/files/15047830/out.txt) yields an interesting observation: the prints are styled as following: 

1. Reset style
2. Set foreground (text) to whatever the current colorscheme considers black
3. Set the font to bold
4. (put text)
5. Reset style

Obviously, ~~most~~ many people run a dark colorscheme. And in many cases, for these the background color will be equal to what the colorscheme considers black. So generally speaking, I would advice the following:

- __Never change the foreground color to either black (`30m`) or white (`37m`)__
  - Reason:  these are quite likely to collide with the background color of a given terminal
- It is of course ok to change the foreground color __if__ the background color is changed as well to a different color not equal to the default (`49m`)

Now my personal preference would be to leave the background intact, thus forcing the use of a foregroundcolor  (how about yellow, to indicate a non fatal yet significant problem?) except for black/white for the seL4/microkit generated output, or the use of __bold__ alone (which blends in well with any terminal colorscheme, thus my preference).

As is, the UX is unnecessarily poor for fellow dark-colorscheme users tinkering with the (otherwise excellent!) tutorial, or microkit in general.
